column2: Two questions and two replies retain David's inquiry, divine command and Hebron destination. No second-person divine pronoun needs an archaic form in these first-person questions.
Both wives, their origins and Abigail's identification as Nabal's wife remain in the sentence that continues into verse 3.
The men and each household share the ascent and settle in Hebron's cities, plural; no single residence replaces them.
Judean men anoint David over Judah's house, then report Saul's burial by Jabesh's men; the kingship is not yet stated over all Israel.
The message is to Jabesh's leaders and blesses mercy toward their human lord Saul, the Lord's anointed; both Saul and Jonathan are named as buried.
The wish for divine mercy and truth differs from David's future commitment to good things; the causal link to their action remains.
Strong hands and becoming men of valour preserve the exhortation, followed by Saul's death and Judah's anointing of David over themselves.
Abner takes Saul's son from the camp to Mahanaim; inherited Ish-bosheth corresponds here to Iebosthe, not to the distinct Mephibosheth form encountered later.
The six territorial references retain Thasiri and the final all Israel rather than substituting a reconstructed tribal designation.
Forty years of age and two years of rule remain alongside the exception for Judah following David.
column3: The relationship of this duration to David's longer Hebron reign is not harmonized.

column2: Seven years and six months remains the specific Hebron reign over Judah's house; neither the territorial restriction nor the half-year is lost.
Abner and Ish-bosheth's servants move from Mahanaim to Gibeon, preserving the separate royal allegiances.
Joab and David's servants come from Hebron and meet at Gibeon's spring, with the two groups seated on its sides.
column3: This side/that side interprets the paired deictic phrases as contrasting positions; the Greek repeats here without supplying compass directions.

column2: Play remains the proposed action before the commanders and is not silently replaced with a nonlethal sport or an explicit duel to the death.
The twelve from Benjamin belonging to Ish-bosheth and twelve from David's servants remain separately counted before crossing.
Each man's hand grasps the other's head, the sword enters the other's side and they fall together; Portion of the Plotters retains the translated place-name.
column3: Thrust supplies the finite action implicit in the verbless sword clause; no alternative name is substituted.

column2: Very severe battle and defeat of Abner and Israel's men before David's servants retain the collective outcome.
All three sons of Zeruiah are named, with Asahel's light feet compared to a gazelle in the field.
Asahel pursues Abner without turning right or left; repeated following keeps the fixed pursuit clear.
Abner's backward look, identification question and Asahel's first-person reply remain ordinary human dialogue.
Abner offers a right-or-left diversion toward another young man and his full armour; Asahel remains unwilling to turn.
The repeated warning, potential strike to the ground, face-to-Joab question and extra return-to-Joab instruction remain.
column3: Where do these things lead interprets the compressed where are these things question. The wording remains provisional rather than a settled spatial or consequential analysis.

column2: The refusal, spear butt, loins, passage through the back, falling, dying and bystanders stopping are all retained.
column3: Beneath him preserves the difficult local pronoun; no alternative weapon action or medical explanation is supplied.

column2: Joab and Abishai continue pursuit at sunset to Amman facing Gai on Gibeon's desert road; inherited geographical forms remain.
Benjamin's men gather behind Abner as one company atop a hill, retaining the repeated unity rather than adding reinforcements.
The forever-devouring sword question, bitter outcome and failure to order withdrawal from our brothers retain Abner's appeal.
The oath and negative condition remain with early morning and each after his brother.
column3: The inherited counterfactual would have gone up is provisional: reference of spoken, temporal connection and whether going up continues pursuit or withdraws remain unresolved. No until morning or ceasing is silently supplied.

column2: Trumpet, collective withdrawal, no further pursuit of Israel and no continued fighting remain separate actions and negatives.
Westward night travel, Jordan crossing, the entire unnamed stretch and return to camp remain.
column3: The stretch translates a substantivized participle without identifying an otherwise unstated region; geography and sequence remain open.

column2: Joab gathers the people and nineteen servants plus Asahel are counted; the final and Asahel is not absorbed into the nineteen.
column3: The counting verb can be understood in the casualty context, but missing is not separately expressed and is not inserted as a settled lexical gloss.

column2: The three hundred sixty from Benjamin belonging to Abner remain; struck down retains the battle-result reading without changing the number.
Asahel is buried in his father's Bethlehem tomb, while Joab and his men travel all night and meet dawn in Hebron; both locations remain distinct.
